newsitem.title: JAPAN: Notion of Asian oil cartel gets mixed review.
newsitem.headline: Notion of Asian oil cartel gets mixed review.

text.p: While a fledgling proposal for the setting up of an Asian oil-buying cartel is still nestled somewhere deep in the offices of Japan's Trade Ministry, the notion has drummed up talk in energy markets around Asia.

In April, an influential Japanese business group submitted a proposal to Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF) and Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) suggesting the creation of a group that would oversee Asian negotiations with Middle Eastern oil producing countries.
Under the proposal, the group would use Asia's collective buying power to secure better oil price terms and supply security guarantees from the world's biggest producers.
The group would operate under the auspices of the 18-member Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum and be based in Tokyo.
A source at Indonesian state oil company Pertamina was understandably lukewarm on the idea, given the country's membership of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).
"If the group is for energy cooperation it may be OK, but if they want to counter OPEC, it will be impossible to get support from Indonesia," the Pertamina source said.
"As a member of OPEC, Indonesia will try for a good price of crude that is acceptable both for consumers and producers," the source said.
A Chinese oil company official was less equivocal about the plan's chances.
"Japan, Singapore, China, and other countries have their own interests. It's impossible to form an alliance," said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

An executive director of the Australian Petroleum Production and Exploration Association (APPEA) said there could be some benefit for Australia in an APEC-backed buying bloc because Australia imports about 30 percent of its oil requirements. But he said the odds were against the plan.
"I wouldn't think it would have much chance of succeeding, particularly under the umbrella of APEC, given that the large oil producing countries of the United States and Canada are members," he said.

Another senior Australian industry source said Australia, as a minor net exporter of liquids but a major net exporter of energy fuels if coal and uranium are included, wants the highest oil price it can get.

"There are many things they (regional importers) can do together but this is one they could clearly not reach agreement on, so I honestly don't believe it's viable given our different sets of objectives," he said. A Hong Kong government spokeswoman told Reuters: "As far as Hong Kong is concerned, APEC is not a trade bloc nor a negotiating body.

"However, should APEC members want to discuss energy issues, they may bring them up at the relevant working group such as (the) energy working group," she added. A top official from Petron, the largest Philippine refiner, viewed the proposal as too tall an order.
"It will not be easy because each company has its own crude purchasing network," he said.
"We are also talking here of so many oil companies in so many countries. It may be too complicated," he added.

APEC groups Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States.
